ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • 4-day history of intensely pruritic, sore, erythematous rash on chest, hands, and antecubital fossae.  
  • No clear trigger identified; no recent change in soaps, detergents, clothing, or environmental exposure reported.

- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset 4 days ago; persistent and worsening pruritus interfering with sleep and work.  
  • Tried OTC steroid cream last night with no improvement; tried OTC antihistamines previously with minimal benefit.

- ENT symptoms:
  • Denies throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, or facial/lip/tongue swelling.  
  • Denies ear pain/hearing changes and neck pain/swelling.

- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • History of eczema on arms; previously managed with prescription topical steroid and bath/shower additives—effective at that time.  
  • No prior ED visits or epinephrine use.

- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies: none reported.  
  • Current/attempted medications:  
    – OTC “steroid cream” (name/dose/route/frequency not documented).  
    – OTC antihistamine(s) (name/dose/route/frequency not documented).

- Relevant past medical history:
  • Eczema (recurrent).  
  • Asthma in childhood—currently asymptomatic.  
  • No other chronic illnesses.

- Social context:
  • 31-year-old male; lives with several flatmates; employed as a project manager at a pharmaceutical company.  
  • Non-smoker; occasional alcohol (few beers per week).

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Patient reports erythematous, cracked, dry skin on chest, hands, and antecubital areas; no facial involvement. (Video quality poor; clinician states rash “appears quite familiar,” presumed eczema.)
- Airway/breathing: No stridor, wheeze, or respiratory distress reported.
- Mental status: Alert; pruritus causing sleep disturbance but no confusion/dizziness.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person: None noted during call.

Assessment:
- Likely eczema flare-up (atopic dermatitis) with new distribution (chest/hands) and marked pruritus.  
  • Justification: Known history of eczema, dry/cracked erythematous rash, severe itch, absence of systemic or ENT allergic features, partial response to prior topical steroids.  
- No evidence of acute allergic airway compromise or anaphylaxis.

Plan:
1. Pharmacologic management  
   • Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid (specific agent/strength per formulary) with clear application instructions.  
   • Prescribe emollient bath/shower additives and regular moisturizer for daily use.  
   • Prescribe non-sedating oral antihistamine Fexofenadine (dose/route/frequency not documented) to reduce itch; advise trial despite limited response to prior OTC antihistamine.  

2. Non-pharmacologic / education  
   • Maintain diary of potential irritants or triggers (soaps, detergents, fabrics, activities).  
   • Avoid hot showers and harsh soaps; use fragrance-free products.  
   • Keep nails short to prevent excoriation; consider cotton gloves at night if scratching during sleep.

3. Follow-up  
   • Reassess in 7–10 days; sooner if rash spreads, becomes infected (pus, increased pain, fever), or if new ENT/allergic symptoms develop (throat tightness, lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty).  
   • If no improvement, consider dermatology referral and/or patch testing.

4. Emergency advice  
   • Seek immediate medical attention (call emergency number) for any breathing difficulty, sudden facial/throat swelling, voice change, or dizziness/syncope.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing/expected elements: Exact names/doses of OTC steroid and antihistamines; detailed skin examination findings; vitals; documentation of potency/class of prescribed steroid; availability of moisturizers at home; vaccination status not discussed.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Audio intermittently unclear; some dialogue clipped, but clinically relevant information obtained.
